how-much-to-charge-for-an-epoxy-garage-f.text:
← Epoxy garage floor bid calculator

How much to charge for an epoxy garage floor

Charge for the grind, not the brochure. A two-car slab is usually about 400 square feet. Full-broadcast flake with a topcoat is not the same job as a solid-color 2-coat, and neither is a job if you only etch the concrete.

The number that sinks underpriced bids is prep. Diamond grinding a 400 sq ft floor at a realistic 80 sq ft per hour is five hours before anyone opens a kit. Coats then run on the billable area — the slab plus waste — because roller loss and cut-in eat material the brochure coverage ignores. Full-broadcast flake is typically 0.15–0.25 lb per square foot; contractors who “guess a couple of bags” buy more on the way back.

Then add cracks and pits as extra hours and extra fill, add the drive as loaded labor plus vehicle miles, mark up overhead on that direct cost, and take margin as a share of the price you send. A $4/sq ft special on a two-car flake grind is often below walk-away before the first bag of flake.

Open the calculator with a default 20×20 full-flake grind. Switch prep to degrease-only or type $1,600 as the price you are considering to see the cheap special fail in the numbers.

Common questions

How much to charge for an epoxy garage floor?

Price the grind, the coats with waste, the flake you actually broadcast, crack and pit patch, travel, overhead, and the margin you intend to keep. A flat dollars-per-square-foot special that skips mechanical prep is how a two-car job comes back as a peel.

Why do $4 per square foot epoxy specials lose money?

They usually assume degrease-only prep and ignore travel, flake bags, and payroll burden. Full diamond grind on a 400 sq ft slab is often as many hours as the coats.

No warranty. This page is not legal, tax, financial, engineering, or business advice, and it does not tell you what to charge. Outputs are arithmetic on your inputs. Verify them before you bid.

how-much-to-charge-for-polyaspartic-gara.text:
← Epoxy garage floor bid calculator

How much to charge for a polyaspartic garage floor

Polyaspartic is not epoxy plus a round number. The kit is more expensive per square foot. Coat hours usually drop because a 1-day flake system is fewer coats and a faster recoat. The grind does not change. If you diamond-profile a 400 sq ft two-car, those hours are still on the ticket.

Homeowners pay for same-day return-to-service and hot-tire resistance. Shops lose money when they price that premium as “epoxy plus $2/sq ft” and forget flake bags, moisture barrier, or a 40-mile drive. Travel is loaded wage times hours on the road, plus vehicle miles — the same way an epoxy bid should have counted it.

Open the calculator, switch the system to 1-day polyaspartic flake, and compare it to full-broadcast epoxy on the same slab. The kit line goes up; the coat-hour line goes down; walk-away is the number to hold when someone asks you to “just do it for epoxy money.”

Common questions

How much to charge for polyaspartic garage floor coating?

Polyaspartic kits cost more per square foot than epoxy, but coat hours drop because a 1-day system usually uses fewer coats and a faster recoat. The grind does not get cheaper. Price kit, flake, prep, travel, and margin separately rather than adding a flat premium to an epoxy number.

Is polyaspartic just expensive epoxy?

No. Same-day return-to-service is the product the homeowner is buying. The shop still has to grind, still has to broadcast flake, and still has to drive there. Skipping any of those and calling it polyaspartic is how a premium ticket still loses money.

No warranty. This page is not legal, tax, financial, engineering, or business advice, and it does not tell you what to charge. Outputs are arithmetic on your inputs. Verify them before you bid.

FOR GARAGE-FLOOR COATING CONTRACTORS

Bid the grind, the flake, and the drive.

Price how much to charge for an epoxy garage floor — or a 1-day polyaspartic flake job — from the hours it takes to profile the slab, the flake you actually broadcast, and the miles to the driveway. A $4/sq ft special that skips the grind is how a two-car comes back as a peel.

Guides: how much to charge for an epoxy garage floor · how much to charge for polyaspartic · this calculator vs. CoatingOS · this calculator vs. a flat rate per square foot

The slab

Pick the opening, then the system. Width and length stay editable so a 19×21 still-a-two-car is not priced as a 20×20.

Kit and production

Starting kit prices and rates are ballpark figures, not a standard. Replace them with the coverage on your last invoice and a grind timed from your own crew.

Your shop

Payroll burden covers employer taxes, workers’ compensation, and shop insurance. Pricing off the raw wage is how a flake job that looked like $9/sq ft was actually $6.

Where the hours go

    Transparent arithmetic from your own inputs. Kit prices and grind rates are starting points, not a standard, a benchmark, or a warranty — time your crew and replace them.

    Hand the customer a proposal

    The price above is for you. This is the page you print or save as a PDF and give to the customer — your details, their details, the scope, the deposit split, and a line for them to sign. Your business details are saved on this device so you only type them once; the customer’s details are never saved.

    Everything on the printed page is text you typed or a number this calculator worked out. It contains no warranty, lien, or cancellation wording — those depend on your jurisdiction and your contract, and this tool is not the place to invent them.

    Common questions

    Why does skipping the grind make a $3/sq ft special come back as a peel?

    Because epoxy and polyaspartic coatings bond to a mechanically profiled surface, not a smooth slab. Degrease-or-acid-etch-only prep is the fastest and cheapest prep option here, but it does not open the concrete’s surface the way a diamond grind or shot blast does. A coating applied over an un-profiled slab can look fine on install day and start peeling within a season — the callback costs far more than the grind would have.

    Why does full-broadcast flake cost more than a solid-color coat?

    It is three coats instead of two, higher waste (12% versus 8%), and slower coverage per hour (220 sq ft versus 300), on top of the flake itself. The flake has to be broadcast to refusal and then topcoated, which is a separate pass. A metallic epoxy trades some of that flake material cost for even slower coverage — 180 sq ft per hour — because the metallic pigment has to be worked while wet to get the marbled look.

    Why do cracks and pits get their own line instead of being part of the square footage?

    Because patching a crack or a pit is prep work done before the coating goes down, priced by the linear foot of crack and the square foot of pit rather than by the floor area. A slab with 40 linear feet of cracking is a patch-and-fill job with a coating on top of it, not a clean floor with a coating — the patch labor and material do not show up if the price is only per square foot of floor.

    What counts as a “starved” flake floor?

    Full-broadcast flake typically lands around 0.15–0.25 lb per square foot. Below roughly 0.12 lb per square foot the floor looks thin and patchy rather than fully covered — usually the sign of underbuying flake for the area rather than a deliberate look. The calculator flags this so the material line matches what the finished floor is supposed to look like.

    Is my data uploaded anywhere?

    No account and no network requests — the calculator runs entirely in your browser. A share link encodes only the inputs you choose into the address bar and is never sent to us, and the optional usage counter records only which features were used and the day, never your garage size, wages, or prices.

    What’s the difference between the bid price and the walk-away price?

    The bid price already includes your target margin on top of labor, materials, and overhead. The walk-away price is the total cost underneath it — prep, coating system, flake, crack and pit repair — the point below which the job stops being profitable at all. Typing a price you are considering shows you the margin or the loss before you send it.

    No warranty. This free tool is not legal, tax, financial, engineering, or business advice, and it does not tell you what to charge. It is not a moisture test, a surface-profile specification, or a product warranty. Verify every figure against your own payroll, kit invoices, and a qualified professional before relying on it or submitting a bid. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for loss or damage from its use.

    Nothing leaves your browser. Every number stays on this device. A share link encodes only the inputs you choose into the address bar and is never sent to us. Usage counts are anonymous tallies of which features were used, stored locally, and never include your slab, wages, costs, or prices.

    Pouring a new slab instead of coating an existing garage floor? The concrete bid calculator prices cubic yards, forms, and finish — nothing uploaded.

vs-a-flat-rate-per-square-foot.html.text:
← Epoxy Garage Floor Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. a flat rate per square foot

"$4 a square foot" is not a price for a garage floor — it is a price for one specific coating system and one specific prep, quietly applied to every slab that walks in the door.

What a flat per-foot rate is

A flat rate is the fastest way to quote: multiply the floor's square footage by a number and read off a price. Homeowners shop it because it is easy to compare between bids, and shops use it because it needs no takeoff. It is also the rate a customer holding a flyer or a competitor's website will ask you to match.

The number behind it was set for one job — one coating system, degrease prep only, no cracks, no moisture barrier — and then reused for every garage afterward, whether or not the next slab looks anything like the one the rate was built on.

What this calculator is

This page keeps no account and sends nothing to a server. You enter the garage's square footage, the coating system (solid-color epoxy, full-broadcast flake, metallic, or 1-day polyaspartic), the prep method (degrease, light grind, full diamond grind, or shot blast), any cracks, pits, or a moisture barrier, and your loaded labor and overhead. It converts prep and coating into hours by rate, adds flake pounds by billable area and waste, and returns a walk-away price below which the job loses money — for this slab, not a generic one.

What a flat per-foot rate doesWhat this calculator does instead
Charges the same $/sq ft whether the job is a degrease-only solid-epoxy coat or a full-diamond-grind full-broadcast flake system — a several-times difference in prep and material for the same floor area. Prices each coating system's own kit cost, coat count, and coat-hour rate, and each prep method's own hours per square foot, so the number tracks the job actually described, not the floor plan alone.
Prices "the garage" as one coated area, with no separate line for cracks, pits, or a moisture barrier. Times cracks at hours and fill per lineal foot, pits at fill per square foot, and a moisture barrier at the full slab area once, so that scope shows up instead of being absorbed into the coated area or skipped.
Assumes degrease-only prep is enough, so a slab needing a full diamond grind gets quoted the same as one that does not. Adds prep hours only for the method actually selected, so a degrease-only job and a full-grind job price differently — about $1,743 walk-away versus about $2,073 once a full diamond grind is added on the same 400 sq ft two-car, while a flat $4-a-square-foot quote on that same slab comes to $1,600.
Guesses flake as "a couple of bags" rather than pricing the billable area. Converts billable square feet (coated area plus waste) into flake pounds from the system's own lb-per-square-foot figure, so the kit invoice the flake bill matches is the one the calculator priced.
Gives the crew a price to quote, not a number to check a quote against. Reports the walk-away price, the effective hourly rate, and the price per square foot, so a shopped price can be scored against real cost before the crew commits to it.

A flat rate is not wrong because it is simple — it is wrong when it is applied outside the one job it was built for, and nothing about a flyer rate tells you when that has happened. This calculator does not replace judgment about your market; it replaces the arithmetic a flat rate skips.

Common questions

Why does a flat rate per square foot get an epoxy garage floor wrong?

Because prep hours and coating system drive the cost, not the floor area alone. A degrease-only solid-epoxy job and a full-diamond-grind flake job on the same 400 square foot two-car differ by hours of grinding and a heavier kit before a single coat goes down. A flat rate charges both the same and is wrong on one of them every time.

What does a flat rate usually leave out entirely?

The grind, the cracks, and which coating system was actually quoted. Solid-color epoxy, full-broadcast flake, metallic, and 1-day polyaspartic each carry a different kit cost per square foot and a different coat-hour rate, and a full diamond grind to profile is often as many hours as the coats themselves. A rate built around "square feet of garage" has nowhere to put any of that.

What happens when the flyer price assumes degrease-only but the slab needs a real grind?

A $4-a-square-foot flyer on a 400 square foot two-car comes to $1,600. This calculator's walk-away price for that same slab with degrease-only prep and a solid-color epoxy kit is about $1,743 once loaded labor, kit cost, and overhead are counted — already short of the flyer rate — and about $2,073 once a full diamond grind to profile is added, which is the prep the trade recommends before a durable coat. The flyer rate is already tight on the lighter job and underwater on the one the slab actually needs.

Is a flat rate ever the right way to quote?

For a narrow band of near-identical jobs — same coating system, same prep, no cracks or pits, no moisture barrier — a flat rate can land close. The risk is applying it outside that band without noticing, because the postcard rate does not know which band a given garage is in and neither does the crew until the slab is profiled.

Does this calculator know what to charge in my market?

No. It has no data on local rates, kit prices, or what competitors charge. It takes the wage, kit cost, and overhead you enter and turns them into a walk-away price for the system, prep, and scope you describe — the arithmetic a flat rate skips, not a market survey.

Nothing here says or implies that quoting a flat rate per square foot is a bad-faith practice — it is a common, honest shortcut that works until the job stops matching the one the rate was set on. This page describes where that shortcut breaks down, not a fault in anyone who uses it. The $1,743, $2,073, and $1,600 figures above are this calculator's own arithmetic on the example job described in its README, not a claim about any specific contractor's real costs.

Open the Epoxy Garage Floor Bid Calculator and price your own job.

No warranty. This free page is not construction, legal, tax, or financial advice, and it does not tell you what to charge or whether a slab needs a full grind. Verify every figure against your own costs and a qualified professional before relying on it or submitting a bid. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for any loss or damage arising from its use.

Best-effort hosting, no SLA. This tool is free and experimental, and may be slow, broken, moved, or taken offline without notice. We do not promise uptime, backups of anything you type, or that a URL will keep working. Do not use it as a system of record.

Everything on this page and on the calculator runs in your browser. Nothing you type is ever sent anywhere.

This calculator vs. CoatingOS

Two different shapes: CoatingOS is a subscription business-management app for running a coating company's estimates, scheduling, invoicing, and customer records. This page is a free, private worksheet for one question — what should this one slab cost, given its grind hours, flake, and kit, before you quote it.

What each tool is for

CoatingOS is an all-in-one business management app built specifically for floor coating contractors — epoxy, polyurea, polyaspartic, and concrete coating professionals. It lets a contractor create and send estimates, convert an accepted estimate into a work order, generate invoices and track payments, schedule jobs, store customer records, send two-way SMS to customers, document jobs with photos, and take deposits through a Square integration. It is sold as an ongoing subscription account with a free trial offered on its own site. CoatingOS's own pricing page is not reachable from this session to confirm today's exact plan names or dollar figures, so no price for it is invented here: only its well-documented identity and category — coating-industry business-management software, sold as a subscription account — are stated, and no dollar amount for CoatingOS appears on this page.

This calculator does none of what CoatingOS does. It does not manage customer records, schedule crews, or send invoices, and it stores no customer or job record on a server. It takes one slab's square footage, grind hours, flake load and coverage, coat count, a choice between full-broadcast epoxy and 1-day polyaspartic kits, waste, crack repair, moisture-barrier treatment, loaded wage, payroll burden, overhead, target margin, and travel, and turns that into the per-job price, the price per square foot, and the walk-away price below which a cut-rate special loses money — plus, if you already have a price on the table, a check of whether it clears that walk-away floor, and a single printable customer proposal for that one job. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and uploads nothing you type.

Should I use this calculator or CoatingOS?

They do different jobs, and a garage-floor coating business of any size may end up using both.
